title: Retiring, still serving
hook: leaving paid work and continuing to serve
tomorrow: the wedding budget fight. can three old words settle it?

segments.voice: Yesterday, losing work: Bebe said take it sweetly, Harjit said start tonight, and chardi kala held them both. Rise anyway. Today, someone leaves work on purpose.

Diesel, burnt coffee, and the hiss of air brakes. That's what the yard smells and sounds like at six in the morning, and Chacha Balwinder, Jasleen's dad, has known it longer than Simran has been alive. Today is his last shift driving for Harjit's company. The drivers clap him out of the yard. Somebody honks a horn too long. Then, in the parking lot, he hands Harjit his keys and says the thing nobody expects. Tomorrow at six he'll be somewhere else. Where?
screen: `DIESEL, COFFEE, AIR BRAKES.` → `A LAST SHIFT, AND A HANDED-OVER KEY.` → `TOMORROW AT SIX, WHERE?`

segments.voice: The answer has a different smell: onions in hot oil, cardamom tea, and the clatter of stacked steel trays. Chacha's new six a.m. is the gurdwara langar kitchen. Sikhi has no word for stopping serving. Paid work can end. Seva, selfless service, doesn't retire. On ang 26, Guru Nanak says, in paraphrase, serve in this world, and you will be given a seat in the Lord's court. Service isn't a phase of life; it's the shape of it. And here's one to tell a friend tonight. Tradition says Guru Amar Das came to Guru Angad late in life, an old man by then, and served him anyway, carrying water before dawn, in heat and rain. The one who served became the third Guru. So the tradition doesn't picture old age as sitting still. It pictures hands that keep moving, at a gentler pace. Not everyone can stand at a tava for hours, and seva doesn't ask that. It can be folding chairs, sitting with the sick, teaching a grandchild Gurmukhi, reading Gurbani to someone whose eyes have dimmed. Chacha's hands, which held a wheel for years, now hold a ladle. He says the dal is harder to steer.
screen: `ONIONS, TEA, STEEL TRAYS.` · `PAID WORK ENDS; SEVA DOESN'T.` · `ANG 26: SERVE IN THIS WORLD.` · `GURU AMAR DAS, CARRYING WATER.` · then, large: `KEEP SERVING.`

segments.voice: Rest your hands on your knees, palms up, and look at them for a while: the lines, the knuckles, any scars or calluses they've picked up. Think of a few things they've carried for other people over the years. Then close them gently and keep that weight in mind as you sit, and one thing these hands might still carry for someone, years from now.
Retiring. Leaving paid work, and in Sikhi, carrying on with seva at whatever pace the body allows.
Keep serving: the paycheck stops, the seva doesn't, and Chacha starts at six tomorrow, ladle in hand. Day done.
